Hi! So every device you use — your phone, a kettle, Christmas lights — works because charge flows around a circuit and transfers energy. Today we're starting with electric current, which is just the rate at which that charge flows.

What do you think "rate of flow" means in everyday language?

turns.student: like how fast water comes out of a tap?
turns.reply:
Exactly right! So current works the same way — it's how much electric charge flows past a point every second, and we measure it in amperes.

How much charge flows past a point in a circuit that has a current of 1 ampere, every second?

Right — 1 coulomb per second is exactly what 1 ampere means, so you've got it!

Now, when charge flows around a circuit, it transfers energy. Potential difference tells you how much energy gets transferred for each coulomb of charge that flows.

What unit do we measure potential difference in?
recap: Electric current is the rate at which electric charge flows around a circuit.
We measure current in amperes, which tells us how much charge passes each second.
One ampere means one coulomb of charge flows past a point every second.
Current transfers energy to devices like phones, kettles, and lights to make them work.

turns.reply:
Think of it like this: when charge moves through a circuit, it carries energy along with it. Potential difference tells you how much energy each bit of charge is carrying — it's the energy per coulomb. We measure it in **volts**.

What happens to the energy when charge flows through a light bulb?

When charge flows through a bulb, it transfers energy to the wire, which heats up and makes light.

Now, some components fight against the flow of charge — we call that **resistance**, and it's measured in ohms. What do you think happens to the current if a circuit has more resistance?
recap: Potential difference measures how much energy each coulomb of charge carries.
We measure potential difference in volts.
When charge flows through something like a bulb, it transfers that energy.

turns.reply:
Resistance is like a blockage in the circuit — it slows down the charge flowing through, so less current gets through.

What happens to the current when resistance gets bigger?

Right — when resistance gets bigger, current gets smaller. We measure resistance in a unit called the **ohm**, written as Ω. If a component has a potential difference of 6 volts across it and a current of 2 amps flowing through it, what is its resistance?

turns.student: is it like 6 plus 2? so 8 ohms?
turns.reply: Not quite — it's division, not addition. Now, when you want to see how a component really behaves, you can plot a graph showing how current changes as you increase the potential difference across it — that's called an **I-V characteristic graph**. What do you think the axes of that graph would be?
recap: Resistance is the opposition to current flowing through a circuit, measured in ohms.
When resistance increases, the current flowing through decreases — they work opposite ways.
Current loses energy pushing through resistance, which is why wires heat up.

turns.reply: An I-V characteristic graph just shows you two things on a graph — how current changes when you turn up the potential difference on a component. What two things go on the axes of that graph?

turns.student: um current and voltage? on the y and x?
turns.reply: Exactly — current on the y-axis, voltage on the x-axis. When you plot a fixed resistor at constant temperature, the graph makes a straight line through the middle point. Why would the line be straight?

turns.student: cuz resistance stays the same so current always goes up the same amount?
turns.reply: A **diode** is a component that only lets current flow in one direction — we call that the forward direction. In the reverse direction, it has a very high resistance, so only a tiny current flows through it. What do you think that means for the shape of a diode's I-V graph in the reverse direction?
Shall I just tell you what happens with a diode's graph in the reverse direction?

In reverse, a diode has very high resistance, so almost no current flows through it — the graph stays flat near the bottom. What do you think changing the variable resistor would do to the current flowing through the circuit?
recap: An I-V characteristic graph plots current (y-axis) against voltage (x-axis) to show how a component really behaves.
A fixed resistor gives a straight line because its resistance stays constant, so current increases evenly.
A diode only lets current flow one way (forward direction) and blocks it the other way (reverse direction).

In the practical, you measure the current using an ammeter, which you connect in series with the component — that means it goes in the same loop as the component, so all the charge flows through it.

Where in the circuit do you connect the ammeter?

An ammeter is the meter that measures current, and you have to put it in the same loop as the component so all the charge flows through it—that's what we call connecting it in series.

What does "in series" mean?

An ammeter measures current and goes in series — in the same loop as the component. A voltmeter measures potential difference and connects in parallel, which means it goes across the component without breaking the loop. You've got the basics of current and how to measure it — that's a solid start.
